questions.prompt: An assertion is signed but not encrypted. Which protection does a properly verified signature provide?

options.text: Integrity and authentication of the protected content under the trusted signing key
options.explanation: Verification links the protected content to the expected signer and detects unauthorized changes.

options.text: Secrecy of every attribute from anyone holding the XML
options.explanation: Signing does not hide readable content.

options.text: Automatic authorization for all resources
options.explanation: A signature does not define the application's access policy.

options.text: Guaranteed deletion of every browser copy
options.explanation: A signature does not erase captured data.

questions.prompt: Atlas decrypts an assertion with its private key. What protection is encryption primarily intended to provide?

options.text: Confidentiality of the encrypted content for the intended recipient
options.explanation: Encryption limits readability, while issuer authenticity and acceptance require additional checks.

options.text: Proof that every field outside the encrypted assertion is trusted
options.explanation: Protection applies to the relevant layer, not arbitrary surrounding fields.

options.text: Proof that the user has an active Atlas account
options.explanation: Account eligibility is not a cryptographic decryption result.

options.text: A permanent replacement for HTTPS
options.explanation: Transport protection remains important even when XML content is encrypted.

questions.prompt: Okta signs assertions sent to Atlas. Who should hold the signing private key?

options.text: Okta's signing infrastructure
options.explanation: The signer controls the private key; Atlas verifies using independently trusted public-key material.

options.text: Every user's browser
options.explanation: Browsers should not receive the provider's signing private key.

options.text: Atlas's public metadata file
options.explanation: Metadata distributes appropriate public material rather than the signing private key.

options.text: Atlas's verification service
options.explanation: The receiver needs trusted public material for verification, not control of the sender's signing private key.

questions.prompt: Okta encrypts assertions for Atlas. Which key arrangement fits that direction?

options.text: Okta uses Atlas's encryption public key; Atlas holds the corresponding private key
options.explanation: Recipient key ownership allows the recipient to decrypt without sharing its private key.

options.text: Okta encrypts using Atlas's private key obtained from the browser
options.explanation: The recipient's private key should remain under recipient control.

options.text: Atlas decrypts using Okta's signing certificate alone
options.explanation: The provider's signing public key is not Atlas's decryption private key.

options.text: Atlas decrypts using its public encryption certificate alone
options.explanation: Public recipient material allows encryption to the recipient; decryption requires the corresponding private-key capability.

questions.prompt: An untrusted incoming assertion includes a certificate in KeyInfo. How should Atlas treat it?

options.text: As message-supplied material that must not establish trust by itself
options.explanation: The receiver needs an independently established trust anchor or approved key resolution policy.

options.text: As automatic authority to authenticate any issuer
options.explanation: An attacker can include a certificate in a message.

options.text: As proof the browser authenticated the issuer
options.explanation: The browser does not make an embedded signing key trusted.

options.text: As a replacement for checking the expected issuer
options.explanation: Even a usable verification key must be associated with the expected trusted provider and integration.

questions.prompt: An engineer compares a new signing certificate's fingerprint with a value received through an authenticated change process. Why?

options.text: To confirm the intended public key material before trusting it
options.explanation: Fingerprint comparison is useful only when the expected value comes through an appropriate trusted channel.

options.text: To decrypt every assertion with the fingerprint
options.explanation: A fingerprint is a digest identifier, not a decryption key.

options.text: To establish that the certificate was active when the assertion was issued
options.explanation: A matching fingerprint identifies material; activation timing requires separate issuance and configuration evidence.

options.text: To prove the application has refreshed all nodes
options.explanation: Identity of the file and runtime adoption are separate facts.

questions.prompt: Only the Assertion is signed. Which content is directly protected by that assertion signature?

options.text: The referenced assertion content within the verified signature scope
options.explanation: An assertion signature does not automatically cover surrounding Response fields.

options.text: Every HTTP header on the POST
options.explanation: The XML signature does not cover arbitrary transport headers.

options.text: Any separate RelayState form value automatically
options.explanation: A separate binding field is outside the assertion signature's scope.

options.text: Every sibling Assertion in the same Response
options.explanation: A signature protects its actual references and scope, not every neighboring XML object.

questions.prompt: A receiver verifies one Assertion but builds the user session from another unsigned Assertion in the same document. What is wrong?

options.text: The application consumed identity data from an object it did not authenticate
options.explanation: The trusted, verified object must be the one used for identity and access decisions.

options.text: Nothing, because any signature covers every sibling element
options.explanation: Signature coverage follows references and transforms, not mere proximity.

options.text: The unsigned assertion is acceptable if it names the same issuer
options.explanation: A claimed issuer string does not authenticate the second object or bind consumption to the verified assertion.

options.text: The XML must simply be Base64-encoded again
options.explanation: Encoding does not repair consuming unverified content.

questions.prompt: A message's digest matches after processing its signature references. Is that alone enough to trust the issuer?

options.text: No; the signature must also verify under the expected trusted key and allowed processing rules
options.explanation: Content digest agreement is only part of signature validation and trust evaluation.

options.text: Yes; any matching digest identifies the intended IdP
options.explanation: A digest does not establish who is trusted to sign.

options.text: Yes; a matching digest means the embedded certificate is trusted
options.explanation: Digest correctness does not establish independent trust in the key supplied with the message.

options.text: No; SAML never uses digests
options.explanation: XML signatures use digests, but those digests are not a complete trust decision.

questions.prompt: Why do XML signatures use defined canonicalization and transforms?

options.text: To derive the specified representation of referenced XML for signature processing
options.explanation: Both sides need precise processing rules. Canonicalization is not permission to consume a different object.

options.text: To decide which local account matches the signed NameID
options.explanation: Canonicalization concerns cryptographic XML representation, not account-resolution policy.

options.text: To encrypt all visible XML tags
options.explanation: Canonicalization does not provide encryption.

options.text: To make every modified XML document acceptable
options.explanation: Unauthorized modifications can still invalidate the protected content.

questions.prompt: A receiver can technically process an old signature algorithm that the integration's security policy disallows. What should it do?

options.text: Enforce its approved algorithm policy
options.explanation: Parser or library capability does not make every available algorithm acceptable.

options.text: Accept any algorithm that decodes
options.explanation: Decoding and cryptographic policy are different checks.

options.text: Let the browser choose a weaker algorithm after failure
options.explanation: The browser should not override receiver policy.

options.text: Ignore the signature whenever an algorithm is unfamiliar
options.explanation: The correct response is controlled rejection, not skipping protection.

questions.prompt: Why is successful decryption alone insufficient to trust an assertion's issuer?

options.text: Anyone able to obtain the recipient's public encryption key may be able to encrypt content for that recipient
options.explanation: Encryption to a recipient is not, by itself, authentication of the expected sender.

options.text: Only the genuine IdP can ever know an SP's public key
options.explanation: Public-key material is intentionally distributable.

options.text: Decryption always validates audience and replay state
options.explanation: Those are separate acceptance checks.

options.text: Encryption forces the SP account to exist
options.explanation: Encryption has no such lifecycle effect.

questions.prompt: A Response signature correctly covers the Response and its nested Assertion. May the SP consume identity from an unrelated unsigned XML object elsewhere?

options.text: No; identity must come from the object authenticated by the verified protection scope
options.explanation: A valid envelope signature is useful only when processing remains bound to the content it protects.

options.text: Yes, if the unrelated object has a familiar display name
options.explanation: Familiar text does not authenticate an XML object.

options.text: Yes, because the whole browser tab is signed
options.explanation: XML signatures do not sign browser tabs.

options.text: Yes, if both objects contain the same subject identifier text
options.explanation: Matching text does not extend a signature's coverage to an unrelated unsigned object.

questions.prompt: Okta will begin signing with K2 instead of K1. What should happen before activation when the SP supports overlapping trusted keys?

options.text: Distribute and verify K2 trust across the actual validating receivers
options.explanation: Preparing receiver trust before issuance switches prevents rejection of the new signatures.

options.text: Remove K1 everywhere before distributing K2
options.explanation: That can leave no usable trust during the transition.

options.text: Send K2's private key to the SP
options.explanation: Verification requires public material, not the provider's private key.

options.text: Change only the user's display name
options.explanation: User profile labels do not configure signature trust.

questions.prompt: A load-balanced SP has K2 installed on two nodes but not a third. What symptom is plausible after issuance switches to K2?

options.text: Intermittent signature failures depending on the validating node
options.explanation: Configuration must be adopted by every active validator, not merely saved centrally.

options.text: All nodes necessarily succeed because the browser caches K2
options.explanation: Browser caching does not update server-side trust stores.

options.text: The provider's successful issuance guarantees every node can verify
options.explanation: Issuance and effective verification trust at each receiving runtime are separate requirements.

options.text: Every failure must be an expired assertion
options.explanation: The stated node-specific trust mismatch points to verification, not necessarily to time conditions.

questions.prompt: When is retiring K1 most defensible during a planned, uncompromised signing rollover?

options.text: After confirming K2 adoption and the agreed overlap and outstanding-message handling
options.explanation: Retirement should follow actual receiver readiness and the transition's defined acceptance window.

options.text: Immediately when a new file is downloaded
options.explanation: Downloading does not prove activation or adoption.

options.text: Never; every historical key must remain trusted forever
options.explanation: Indefinite trust is not a controlled rollover policy.

options.text: After one user reaches an app page using an old local session
options.explanation: An existing session may bypass federation and therefore does not prove new-key adoption.

questions.prompt: The signature result and consumed identity refer to different assertions. What is the first defect to address?

options.text: The receiver consumed an identity object it did not authenticate
options.explanation: Validation must remain bound to the exact object used for the identity decision.

options.text: The audience check alone should be removed
options.explanation: That would weaken a separate acceptance boundary.

options.text: The unsigned assertion should inherit trust from its sibling
options.explanation: Proximity in XML does not establish signature coverage.

options.text: The browser should Base64-encode both assertions together
options.explanation: Transport encoding does not authenticate the consumed object.

evidence: Consumed NameID comes from unsigned Assertion _B

questions.prompt: Atlas successfully decrypts the packet, but has no issuer verification result. What remains unknown?

options.text: Whether the content is authenticated under the expected issuer trust
options.explanation: Recipient confidentiality and sender authenticity are different properties.

options.text: Whether Atlas obtained readable XML
options.explanation: Successful decryption establishes that stated result.

options.text: Whether the private decryption key was usable for this packet
options.explanation: The recorded operation establishes its use for this decryption.

options.text: Whether encryption automatically validates audience
options.explanation: It does not; audience remains a separate check rather than a decryption result.

evidence: Audience and account result: not supplied

questions.prompt: The observations below follow K2 activation. What best explains the supplied intermittent signature failures?

options.text: One active validator has not adopted K2
options.explanation: The effective node inventory and node-specific results identify a trust-adoption mismatch.

options.text: The audience is necessarily wrong on every node
options.explanation: The packet supplies matching audiences and successful acceptance at A.

options.text: The user's password changes between nodes
options.explanation: The supplied failure is signature verification after issuance.

options.text: K2 is necessarily invalid everywhere
options.explanation: Successful verification at A contradicts that universal conclusion.

evidence: Issuer switched from approved K1 to K2
Node A trusts K2 and verifies; node B trusts only K1 and fails
Audience and ACS match the test contract

questions.prompt: An SP pins a SAML signing certificate through authenticated metadata. What should an engineer avoid assuming?

options.text: That SAML key trust is automatically identical to ordinary browser HTTPS certificate validation
options.explanation: Federation deployments can use metadata or explicit trust configurations rather than the browser's public Web PKI decision model.

options.text: That the public key can verify a signature
options.explanation: That is its intended verification role.

options.text: That the issuer must be checked
options.explanation: Issuer checks remain necessary.

options.text: That changes need a controlled process
options.explanation: A controlled trust update is appropriate.
